newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK Telecom stake speculation revived.
newsitem.headline: HK Telecom stake speculation revived.

text.p: Shares in Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd have risen sharply on speculation it is seeking a mainland Chinese partner, analysts said on Wednesday.
The rumours of a mainland investor have resurfaced less than two months before Hong Kong reverts to China.
Hongkong Telecom's share price was up HK$0.15 at HK$14.25 at 0700 GMT on Wednesday, not far from its high for the year of HK$14.60.
Salomon Brothers analyst Dan Sherman said the prospect of China's Ministry of Post and Telecommunications (MPT) investing in Hongkong Telecom was not new.
"The idea's there, and I think both sides think the idea's interesting and would like to figure out some way to do it that might give both sides a big advantage," Sherman said.
Hongkong Telecom said it had nothing to say.
"If it's market rumour, then we won't comment," said a spokeswoman for the company, which on Thursday reports results for the year to March 31.
Hongkong Telecom is 58.5 percent owned by Cable & Wireless Plc but analysts said it and C&W might see advantages to taking on a mainland partner because of the handover.
Hong Kong reverts to Chinese sovereignty on July 1 after more than 150 years of British rule.
Chinese agencies have stakes in Hong Kong airlines and utility China Light & Power, and the Bank of China has been issuing Hong Kong banknotes for almost four years.
CITIC Pacific last year more than doubled its stake in flagship carrier Cathay Pacific Ltd and China National Aviation Corp bought nearly 36 percent of Hong Kong Dragon Airlines Ltd.
CITIC Pacific, which once held 20 percent of Hongkong Telecom, now holds only eight percent.
Hongkong Telecom's monopoly on international direct dial calls does not expire until 2006 but other operators' call-back services have eaten into its business.
Sherman said an investor might be hesitant to buy until the dust settled.
"Personally, I would like to know what the heck I was buying," Sherman said.
Political factors might override economic factors in any investment decision, analysts said.

"Whilst regarding it as a low probability event, an MPT buy-in cannot be entirely dismissed since it may ultimately be driven by higher-level decision-makers whose primary consideration may well be 'face'," Merrill Lynch said in a report last week.
But it warned that investors holding Hongkong Telecom shares hoping to benefit from a China restructuring might be disappointed.
Analysts said Hongkong Telecom was a far more expensive proposition for a mainland investor than Cathay Pacific or China Light, with more pressure on C&W to take the initiative.
"I think it's something that Cable & Wireless has to do more than the Chinese," said G.K. Goh analyst Philip Wickham.
Hongkong Telecom had been accumulating huge cash reserves, up to HK$11 billion at March 31, so it could move quickly if an opportunity arose in China, Wickham said.
"But the question is: when will China liberalise its telecommunications?" he said, adding that C&W's British lineage did not help Hongkong Telecom.
"That really hurts its chances -- period," Wickham said.
BZW Asia's Lloyd Fischer said a China deal would be seen as positive, but would not necessarily solve all the utility's problems.
